Set
sĕt
v.t. (to place, fix, or appoint; rendering Hebrew shith, sim, Greek tithēmi, histemi)
Saxon settan, causative of sit — to cause to sit, hence to fix in place. Scripture uses it for what God establishes and for what a man deliberately fixes his heart upon.

Biblical Definition

To set is to put a thing deliberately in a place and leave it there, and Scripture uses it for both God's establishing and man's resolving. God sets a rescued man on solid ground: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). God set a joy before His Son: “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Heb 12:2) — the same verb twice, the joy set before Him and the Son now set down, the enduring bracketed by two divine placements. Answering this, the believer is commanded to set: “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:2), and David testifies, “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Psa 16:8). Setting is therefore the deliberate act by which a soul decides in advance where it will look. It is not a mood that visits; it is a placement a man makes and keeps.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines set as to put or place, to fix firmly, to appoint or assign, and to fix the affection or heart upon an object.

expand to see more

SET, v.t. To put or place; to fix or cause to rest in a standing posture.

2. To put or place in its proper or natural posture.

3. To fix; to make fast or firm.

4. To appoint; to assign; as, to set a time.

To set the heart on, to fix the desires on; to love or covet.

Key Scripture

Psa 40:2 — "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings."

Heb 12:2 — "Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God."

Col 3:2 — "Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth."

Psa 16:8 — "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."

Modern Corruption

Devotion has been redefined as feeling that arrives rather than affection a man sets, which leaves the believer waiting on his moods for what Scripture commands him to do on purpose.

expand to see more

“Set your affection on things above” is an imperative, and imperatives assume the thing can be done whether or not one feels like doing it. Much modern piety assumes the reverse: that love for God is a weather system, and that the honest response to a cold heart is to wait for warmth. Scripture treats the affections as steerable — they follow what a man deliberately puts before his eyes. David does not report a feeling; he reports a placement: I have set the LORD always before me. The feeling followed, and so did the stability.

Hebrews shows the same mechanism in the Lord Himself. He endured the cross for a joy that was set before Him — that is, He held a future gladness in view and let it carry Him through present shame. This is not stoicism, which denies the shame, nor is it sentiment, which waits for the shame to stop hurting. It is a deliberate setting of the mind on what is real above, and it is exactly what Colossians commands of every believer under pressure.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shith (H7896) and sim (H7760), to put, place, appoint; Greek tithēmi (G5087), to lay or set, and phroneō (G5426), to set the mind upon.

expand to see more

Hebrew shith (H7896) — to put, set, appoint; “I have set the LORD always before me” (Psa 16:8).

Hebrew sim (H7760) — to place, establish, constitute; used of setting a king and setting a boundary.

Greek phroneō (G5426) — to be minded, to set the mind or affection on; the imperative of Col 3:2.

Usage

"“Set my feet upon a rock” — deliverance described as a placement God makes."

"“Set your affection on things above” — devotion commanded as a deliberate act."

"“For the joy that was set before him endured the cross” — the Lord's own method under shame."
